modalities.name: Inner Roster Games
modalities.tagline: Rotate team roles and meet the inner parts that push back.
modalities.whatItIs: Inner Roster Games is a new, untested concept halfway between recreational team sport and Internal Family Systems, a form of parts work that sees the mind as a family of inner parts. A small group plays relaxed, non-contact games while deliberately rotating through roles such as leading, defending or sitting a round out, then pauses to notice which part reacts to each one.
modalities.coreIdea: Most of us fall into the same role on any team, and the parts that guard it, such as the one that must win or the one that hides, may show up most clearly when we try a different role. Meeting those parts with curiosity in the middle of play, rather than in a therapy room, may make them easier to recognize in everyday life.
modalities.whatYouDo: Eight to twelve people meet in a park for 90 minutes with a facilitator trained in group work and play short rounds of a slow-paced disc or ball game at walking or gentle jogging pace. Before each round everyone takes a role they rarely choose, and afterwards the group huddles for two minutes so each player can name the part that showed up, for example 'a part of me wanted to disappear', without anyone analyzing it. The session ends in a circle where players share what it was like to play from a calmer, more curious place.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who learn better by doing than by talking, and who notice they always end up as the leader, the helper or the one on the sidelines and want to understand what that habit protects.
modalities.cautions: Jogging, turning and catching bring a risk of sprains and knocks, so warm up, keep the game non-contact and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. Old feelings about being picked last or judged can surface, so sharing is always optional, and anyone with severe trauma or in crisis should work with a licensed therapist rather than rely on a game.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Inner Roster Games. A relaxed team game where you swap into roles you usually avoid, then huddle to notice which part of you pushed back. For anyone who always ends up the leader, the helper or the one on the sidelines and wonders why.

modalities.name: The Pacing Council
modalities.tagline: A brisk walk where your inner voices negotiate the pace.
modalities.whatItIs: The Pacing Council is a proposed practice halfway between Internal Family Systems, which sees inner voices as parts with their own intentions, and steady endurance exercise. During a brisk walk, or a gentle walk-jog for fitter people, the voice that pushes you faster and the voice that wants to stop are each heard as a part with its own worries, in time with your steps.
modalities.coreIdea: Steady effort over half an hour or more tends to bring out the same inner pushers and quitters, one after another, which makes a long walk a natural meeting place for them. The aim is to obey neither but to hear what each one fears, and then let a calmer, more curious part of you set the pace.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week you go out for 30 to 45 minutes at a brisk pace where you could still talk easily, after a few first outings alongside a coach or guide trained in parts work, who stays available for check-ins afterward. When a strong voice shows up, such as 'you are too slow' or 'just stop', you ease off slightly and silently ask what it is afraid would happen, letting an answer come in rhythm with your footsteps. Afterwards you spend five minutes noting which voices came, when, and what they seemed to want.
modalities.whoItsFor: Walkers and joggers who hear a harsh inner coach or a voice that always wants to quit, and people who think more clearly on the move than sitting across from someone.
modalities.cautions: Pain, chest discomfort, dizziness or unusual breathlessness are signals to stop, not voices to negotiate with, and anyone with heart or other medical conditions should get medical advice first and build up gradually. If old, painful memories come up strongly, slow down and take them to a trained therapist, since this untested idea is not a substitute for trauma care.
modalities.tweet: An idea for walkers: The Pacing Council. On a brisk walk, the voice that pushes you and the voice that wants to quit become parts with their own fears. Hear each one out, then let your calmer self choose the pace. For anyone with a harsh inner coach.

modalities.name: The Unloading Set
modalities.tagline: Lift a light weight, set it down, and notice what you carry.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unloading Set is a new concept that blends an idea from Internal Family Systems, that inner parts can carry burdens of old beliefs and feelings, with the set structure of strength training. Each set pairs a light physical load with one inner load you name beforehand, and slowly putting the weight down becomes a felt rehearsal of choosing what you keep carrying.
modalities.coreIdea: A weight you can feel in your hands makes the idea of carrying something heavy concrete, and so does the relief of setting it down. Practicing that contrast inside a predictable routine is meant to give protective parts a safe, bodily taste of putting a load down, without forcing a dive into where the burden came from.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you meet a strength coach with training in parts work for a 40-minute session of carries, squats and presses with light weights, in sets of 8 to 10 that stay well short of your limit. Before each set you name one thing a part of you feels it must hold up, such as 'keeping everyone happy', then lift or carry the weight with full attention and set it down slowly, noticing what changes in your hands, shoulders and breath. Between sets you rest, breathe and write one line about what letting go felt like.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they have to hold everything together, and who find it easier to feel a change in the body than to talk one through.
modalities.cautions: Keep the loads light with good technique, breathe out on the effort instead of holding your breath, and get medical advice first if you have high blood pressure or heart or eye problems. Strong emotions can arrive mid-set, so pause whenever you need to, and keep deep trauma work with a licensed therapist, as this untested idea is a complement to care, not a replacement.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: The Unloading Set. Before each set, name something you feel you must hold up, like keeping everyone happy. Lift a light weight, then set it down slowly and notice the relief. For people who always feel they have to hold everything together.

modalities.name: The Patient Brush
modalities.tagline: Groom a calm animal and practice the care a young part needs.
modalities.whatItIs: The Patient Brush is a proposed, therapist-led practice halfway between Internal Family Systems, which sees the mind as made of many inner parts, and animal-assisted therapy. You spend unhurried time grooming a calm, trained dog or horse, and the slow, patient touch the animal responds to becomes a model for approaching the young, hurt parts of yourself.
modalities.coreIdea: An animal tends not to accept being rushed or forced, so caring for one invites, through your hands, the gentle and patient attention that hurt inner parts also seem to need. Once you have felt what that kind of care is like on the outside, it may be easier to offer it on the inside.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a weekly 60-minute session at a farm or clinic, a licensed therapist and a trained animal team guide you as you brush, stroke or simply sit with a calm animal. The therapist helps you notice which part shows up as you approach, such as an impatient one or one that expects rejection, and later invites you to picture offering the same patient touch to a part of you that feels small or scared. The session closes with a few quiet minutes beside the animal and a short talk about what you noticed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are far kinder to animals than to themselves, and people who find it easier to open up with an animal in the room than face to face with a therapist.
modalities.cautions: Allergies, fear of animals, bites, scratches and, around horses, kicks and falls are real risks, so contact is always voluntary and supervised, hygiene rules apply, and the animal gets rest breaks and is free to walk away. Turning toward hurt parts can bring up painful memories, so this untested concept belongs with a licensed clinician and is not suited to a current crisis.
modalities.tweet: What if brushing a calm horse could teach you to be gentle with the hurt parts of yourself? The Patient Brush is a new idea: slow, patient grooming with a therapist nearby, for people who are far kinder to animals than to themselves.

modalities.name: Gathering In
modalities.tagline: A slow closing form that welcomes back every part busy today.
modalities.whatItIs: Gathering In is a new concept halfway between Internal Family Systems, which sees the mind as a family of inner parts, and qigong. Qigong practice often closes by slowly gathering the hands in toward the belly, and here each gathering movement acknowledges one part that was active that day, such as the worrier at breakfast or the critic at work, so the day ends with the whole inner family welcomed rather than only the parts you like.
modalities.coreIdea: Parts work holds that every part means well, even the ones we would rather not have, and qigong ends practice by gathering scattered attention back to the body's center. Ending each day by gathering in every part that showed up, without judging or changing any of them, is meant to build a habit of welcome toward the whole inner family.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly 45-minute sessions, a qigong teacher with training in parts work, or a teacher and a therapist together, teaches the closing form and helps you get to know the parts that show up most, including any that are hard to welcome. At home each evening you stand or sit, recall the day's parts one by one, and for each you sweep your arms slowly outward and gather your hands in to rest on your belly, saying silently something like 'I saw you today'. Anything that stirs strong feelings is left for the next guided session rather than explored alone.
modalities.whoItsFor: People drawn to parts work who want a short, gentle daily ritual, and people who tend to welcome only their 'good' sides and push the rest away.
modalities.cautions: The movements are gentle, but sit for them if standing is tiring, and anyone with a history of psychosis or another serious mental illness should get medical advice before starting qigong. Recalling difficult parts can stir strong feelings, so keep the home ritual light and take deep or traumatic material to a licensed therapist; the concept is untested.
modalities.tweet: Picture ending each day by welcoming back every part of you that showed up: the worrier, the critic, the tired one. Gathering In is a new idea: one slow qigong-style gathering movement for each. For people who only make room for their 'good' sides.

modalities.name: Speak For, Not From
modalities.tagline: Repair small frictions by speaking for the part that reacted.
modalities.whatItIs: Speak For, Not From is a proposed practice for friends, housemates or club members, halfway between Internal Family Systems and everyday socializing. When a small friction happens, you tell the other person about the part of you that reacted, for example 'a part of me felt brushed off', instead of speaking from that part with blame or silence.
modalities.coreIdea: Many clashes between friends run from one person's protective part straight to the other's, which keeps them escalating. Speaking for the part that reacted rather than from it is an idea from Internal Family Systems, and bringing it into ordinary friendships may let small hurts be named early without anyone being cast as the villain.
modalities.whatYouDo: A small circle of friends or housemates learns the method together in a two-hour workshop with a facilitator trained in parts work, who stays available for questions afterward. When something stings, you wait until you feel calmer, then say what happened, which part of you reacted and what it was worried about, such as 'when plans changed, a part of me felt left out, and it worries I don't matter', and the other person says back what they heard and, if they wish, speaks for their own part. Once a month the circle meets for an hour to share how it is going and practice with fresh examples.
modalities.whoItsFor: Friends, housemates or club members who want a kinder way to handle the small hurts that build up between people, and anyone who tends either to explode or to go quiet when stung.
modalities.cautions: This is for everyday frictions between people who basically trust each other, not for relationships that involve abuse, control or threats, where safety and professional support come first. Old, painful feelings can sit behind small hurts, so take those to a trained therapist; the concept is untested.
modalities.tweet: Small friction with a friend? Speak For, Not From is a new idea: instead of blaming or going quiet, you say 'a part of me felt left out, and it worries I don't matter'. Friends learn it together, for hurts that otherwise pile up unspoken.

modalities.name: A Part's Own Place
modalities.tagline: Let a part choose a spot outdoors, and keep it company there.
modalities.whatItIs: A Part's Own Place is a new concept halfway between Internal Family Systems, a form of parts work, and nature walks. On an unhurried walk you invite one inner part, such as a tired protector or a worried younger part, to sense where in the landscape it would like to be, and then you go there and spend time with it.
modalities.coreIdea: Parts work often asks what a part needs, and a real place outdoors gives that question a concrete answer: a sheltered hollow, a high rock with a view, a bench by moving water. Letting the part choose, rather than choosing for it, is a small act of respect that may help it trust you.
modalities.whatYouDo: You walk for 45 to 90 minutes in a quiet park or woodland, at first with a guide trained in parts work who stays available afterward, later alone or with a friend. You bring one part to mind and walk slowly, noticing which paths or spots seem to invite it, and when one does, you go there and sit for ten minutes or so, keeping the part company and asking what it is like for it to be there. Before leaving you thank the part and note in a few words what the place seemed to offer it, such as shelter, a view or the sound of water.
modalities.whoItsFor: People curious about their inner parts who feel more at ease outdoors than in a therapy room, and people who find it easier to sense what they need through places than through words.
modalities.cautions: Plan the route, check the weather, carry water and tell someone where you are going, since slips, heat, cold and getting lost are real outdoor risks. Strong feelings can surface on a quiet walk, so keep deep or traumatic material for sessions with a trained therapist, and use this untested idea as a complement to care, not a replacement.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: if a worried part of you could pick a spot in the woods, where would it go? A Part's Own Place: walk slowly, let the part choose, then sit there and keep it company. For people who sense what they need more easily outdoors.

modalities.name: Clear Window Sitting
modalities.tagline: Your senses as a gauge of how caught up you are.
modalities.whatItIs: Clear Window Sitting is a new concept for a seated practice halfway between Internal Family Systems, a form of parts work, and sensory mindfulness. It uses the plain senses, what you see, hear and feel against the chair, as a gauge of how far an inner part such as worry or anger has taken over your view.
modalities.coreIdea: When a part takes charge, the senses can shift with it: sounds may seem sharper, the visual field narrower, the room less vivid. Noticing how the window of perception clears as the part steps back may give you a concrete, present-moment sign that you are less caught up in it.
modalities.whatYouDo: A guide trained in parts work leads your first three or four sittings and stays available afterward, and then you sit on your own for about 20 minutes in a quiet room. You spend two or three minutes simply looking and listening, then bring to mind a mild, current worry and notice how colors, sounds and the feel of the chair change as the worried part comes forward. You then kindly ask that part to step back a little, look and listen again, and repeat the round two or three times, noting what clears.
modalities.whoItsFor: People drawn to parts work who find it hard to tell from the inside whether a feeling has taken over, and people who prefer concrete sensory anchors to abstract inner work.
modalities.cautions: Use mild, present-day concerns rather than painful memories, and if something strong comes up, open your eyes, feel your feet on the floor and stop. Meditation-style practice can occasionally bring up difficult experiences, so people with a history of trauma, dissociation or psychosis should keep working with a trained therapist rather than sitting alone; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Does the room get louder when you're anxious? Clear Window Sitting, an experimental practice: look and listen, bring up a small worry, notice how sounds and colors change, then ask the worry to step back. A way to sense when a feeling has taken over.

modalities.name: Every Part Plays
modalities.tagline: Give each inner part its own instrument and listen to the ensemble.
modalities.whatItIs: Every Part Plays is a proposed practice halfway between Internal Family Systems, a therapy built around inner parts, and music therapy. With a music therapist, you give each of your parts its own sound on simple instruments, such as a pounding drum for an angry protector or a soft chime for a shy young part, and then let them play together while you listen.
modalities.coreIdea: Some parts have no words, but almost any part can make a sound, and hearing parts play side by side can show how they relate: who drowns out whom, and who never gets a turn. Listening to the whole ensemble from a calm, curious place is a musical way of practicing leading your inner life instead of being run by one part.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a weekly 50-minute session with a credentialed music therapist who knows parts work, you choose a drum, shaker, xylophone or your own voice for two or three parts you already know. You play each part's sound in turn, then the therapist helps you play them together, or plays back a recording of all of them, while you step back, listen and talk about which sound wanted more room. Keeping the recordings from week to week lets you hear how the ensemble changes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to put feelings into words, whether or not they are musical, and people in parts work who want a more expressive, less talk-based way to hear from their parts.
modalities.cautions: Music can stir strong emotions and old memories, so this untested idea belongs with a credentialed music therapist, and with a licensed clinician for any trauma work; it is not suited to a current crisis. Keep the volume moderate to protect your hearing.
modalities.tweet: Imagine giving each part of you an instrument: a loud drum for the angry protector, a soft chime for the shy one. Every Part Plays is a speculative practice where you hear them play together. For people who say more with music than with words.

modalities.name: Check or Carry
modalities.tagline: Sort each sticky thought: test it, or carry it lightly.
modalities.whatItIs: Check or Carry is a new, structured concept halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which tests and changes unhelpful thoughts, and acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), which teaches you to hold them lightly. Instead of using one approach for every thought, you learn to sort each troubling thought into one of two trays: thoughts worth checking against evidence, and thoughts better carried lightly while you get on with what matters.
modalities.coreIdea: Some thoughts are testable predictions that a small experiment can settle, while others are old, sticky stories that arguing with only feeds. The skill at the heart of this method is telling the two apart, so effort goes where it can pay off and acceptance goes where struggle only makes things worse.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over about eight weekly sessions with a therapist, plus a five-minute daily worksheet, you write down one troubling thought and ask two questions: could I test this in the coming week, and has arguing with it ever helped? Checkable thoughts get a small real-life experiment, while thoughts you have argued with a hundred times get a lighter move, such as saying 'I am having the thought that...' and then taking one step you value anyway. Each week you review how the sorting went and adjust it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have tried challenging their thoughts and found that some just bounce back, or who have tried acceptance and wished for something more practical.
modalities.cautions: Generally low risk, though it means regular homework, and the sorting itself can turn into a new way of avoiding hard feelings, which a therapist can help you spot. Severe depression, suicidal thoughts or another serious condition need prompt help from a qualified clinician, and this combined method is untested.
modalities.tweet: Not every anxious thought deserves a debate. Check or Carry is a new concept: sort each sticky thought into 'test it this week' or 'carry it lightly and act anyway'. For anyone whose worst thoughts bounce back however hard they argue.

modalities.name: Old Feeling, New Facts
modalities.tagline: Bring an old feeling fully alive, then meet it with a contradiction.
modalities.whatItIs: Old Feeling, New Facts is a proposed, therapist-led method halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and Coherence Therapy. CBT already tests unhelpful rules with real-life experiments, and this concept borrows Coherence Therapy's insistence that the emotional learning behind a habit first be felt vividly, so that each experiment meets the old feeling while it is fully alive.
modalities.coreIdea: Coherence Therapy, drawing on research into memory reconsolidation, holds that an old emotional learning updates when it is active and meets a clear mismatch at the same moment, not when it is only talked about. The work here is therefore about timing: bring the old feeling fully alive, step straight into an experience that contradicts it, and later check whether the old reaction has quietly stopped firing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Across about ten weekly sessions, you and a licensed therapist start from one habit and follow a chain of questions, such as 'and if that happened, what would it mean about you?', until you reach the feeling-level rule underneath, for example 'needing help means being dropped'. Each experiment is planned in session and starts right there: you recall a moment when the rule felt true until it is vivid, then at once do the contradicting thing, such as phoning a trusted friend to ask for help, while the therapist helps you stay with both. A few weeks later you deliberately revisit situations that used to set the reaction off and note whether it still fires.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with a specific habit that keeps returning despite good coping skills, who like structured, practical steps and want to work at the level where the habit feels necessary, not only at the level of thoughts.
modalities.cautions: Bringing an old emotional learning fully alive can be intense, so this belongs only with a licensed clinician experienced in trauma, especially for anyone with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis. Possible medical causes of a symptom need ruling out first, and the combination is untested, so it should not replace well-tested care for conditions such as major depression or PTSD.
modalities.tweet: Habits can obey old feelings, not just old thoughts. Old Feeling, New Facts is a proposed method: with a therapist, bring the old feeling fully to life, then step straight into an experience that contradicts it. For patterns that survive every tip.

modalities.name: The Clench Swap
modalities.tagline: Catch a hidden tension habit and answer it with a quick shake-out.
modalities.whatItIs: The Clench Swap is a new concept that brings habit reversal, a structured behavioral method used within cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to change automatic habits, together with tension and trauma releasing exercises (TRE). You learn to catch a tension habit you usually miss, such as clenching your jaw or hunching your shoulders, and to answer it each time with a short, deliberate shake-out drawn from tremor practice.
modalities.coreIdea: Habits of bracing run mostly out of sight, so the first step is learning to notice them, which habit reversal trains with cues and self-monitoring, and the second is having a competing move ready. A quick shake-out of the braced area can be done almost anywhere and is meant to interrupt the habit without needing a mat or a full session.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over six weekly 45-minute sessions with a provider trained in both approaches, you pick one tension habit and spend the first week simply noticing when it happens, helped by small reminders such as a dot on your phone screen. You learn a 20-second competing response, such as letting the jaw drop and loosely shaking the shoulders and hands while breathing out, and in each session you also do a short, guided tremor practice so the body knows what letting go feels like. Between sessions you use the shake-out each time you catch the habit, and you review with the provider which moments were hardest to catch.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry tension in one particular place, such as the jaw, shoulders, fists or stomach, and who like a structured, practical method they can use during the working day.
modalities.cautions: Persistent jaw clenching, headaches or pain deserve a check with a doctor or dentist, and anyone with recent injuries should adapt the movements. Tremor practice can stir strong feelings or memories, so people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider alongside their own care; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Clench your jaw or hunch your shoulders without noticing? The Clench Swap is an untested idea: learn to catch the habit, then answer it each time with a 20-second shake-out borrowed from tremor practice. For people who carry stress in one spot.

modalities.name: The Landing Column
modalities.tagline: A balanced thought must fit the facts and feel right inside.
modalities.whatItIs: The Landing Column is a proposed journaling method halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and Focusing. It takes the familiar CBT thought record, where you weigh an upsetting thought against the evidence and write a more balanced one, and adds a final column that asks whether the new thought actually lands in the body.
modalities.coreIdea: A balanced thought that makes sense on paper often fails to feel true, and the 'felt sense' of Focusing, a vague bodily sense of a situation before it is in words, can point to what is missing. Rewording until the thought both fits the evidence and brings a small felt 'yes' joins logical checking with bodily checking.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn the method in a few sessions with a therapist or Focusing-trained coach, who stays available for questions, then use it on your own for about 20 minutes when something upsets you. After writing the situation, the upsetting thought, the evidence and a more balanced alternative, you pause with eyes closed and sense whether the new thought lands, and if it does not, you ask that felt sense what is missing. You rewrite and check again until there is a small sense of relief or fit, then note it in the last column.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who say 'I know it is not true, but it still feels true', and people who like structured tools but want them to reach beyond the head.
modalities.cautions: Usually gentle, but turning inward can bring up strong feelings or memories, and the bodily check should never be used to force yourself into agreeing with a thought. Severe depression, trauma or a current crisis call for a qualified therapist rather than self-help, and this method is untested.
modalities.tweet: Ever written a 'balanced thought' that still felt false? The Landing Column, a new idea: add one last step to your thought journal, close your eyes, and check whether the new thought lands in your body. Keep rewording until something inside says yes.

modalities.name: Hot Thought Coaching
modalities.tagline: Speak from the feeling to find the hot thought, then examine it.
modalities.whatItIs: Hot Thought Coaching is a new concept for one-to-one coaching halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and Aletheia Coaching, a slow, presence-based style. Sessions alternate between speaking from a feeling rather than about it, as Aletheia does, and stepping back to look at the 'hot thought' that came out, the charged belief that CBT tries to catch and check.
modalities.coreIdea: The thought driving a strong reaction often stays hidden while you talk about a situation, and slips out only when you speak from inside the feeling, in words like 'I'm always too much for people'. Catching it in that moment, then stepping back with the coach to look at it calmly, is meant to join Aletheia's depth with CBT's clear-eyed checking.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every two weeks for about three months you meet a coach trained in both styles for 60 minutes. You start with a recent moment that upset you, and the coach slows you down and invites you to speak from the feeling in the first person and the present tense, noticing your tone, pauses and posture, until a sentence comes out that carries the charge; then you both step back, write it down and look at it with a few CBT questions, such as what supports it and what else might be true. You leave with one small step for the next two weeks and repeat the cycle in the next session.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are not in crisis and find that worksheets miss the thought that really drives them, and people who enjoy deep, feeling-led conversation but also want practical tools.
modalities.cautions: This is coaching, not therapy, so the coach must be able to recognize trauma and refer on, and anyone with severe depression, PTSD, suicidal thoughts or another serious condition should work with a qualified mental health professional. Speaking from a feeling can bring up strong emotion, so go at your own pace; the approach is untested.
modalities.tweet: The thought that drives a bad day often slips out only when you speak from the feeling. Hot Thought Coaching, a proposed approach: catch that sentence as it comes, then step back with a coach and look at it calmly. For people worksheets don't reach.

modalities.name: Worry Slot, Empty Slot
modalities.tagline: Fifteen minutes to worry on purpose, then ten minutes to do nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Worry Slot, Empty Slot is a proposed daily practice halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and Do Nothing meditation, a style of sitting whose only instruction is to let whatever happens happen. It pairs CBT's scheduled worry time, a set slot in which you worry on paper on purpose, with a second slot straight afterwards in which you drop all effort and do nothing at all.
modalities.coreIdea: Postponing worries to a set time gives worry a place of its own, but many people then find it hard to stop, so following the worry slot at once with a slot of complete non-doing gives the mind a clear signal that the work is over. Over time the pair is meant to teach that mental effort can be picked up on purpose and then put down.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the method from a CBT practitioner or a workbook, you set two back-to-back slots most days, for example at six in the evening, and jot worries down for later whenever they come during the day. In the 15-minute worry slot you go through them on paper, mark which ones you can act on and plan one step for each, and in the ten-minute empty slot that follows you sit comfortably, let the mind wander and drop any urge to plan, solve or improve anything. Once a week you look back at which worries returned and how the empty slot felt.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose worries spill across the whole day, and who find that even after thinking a problem through they cannot switch off.
modalities.cautions: With nothing to focus on, some people drift back into worry or doze off, and like any meditation, open sitting can occasionally bring up difficult feelings or memories. It is an untested self-help idea, not a form of therapy, so worry that disrupts sleep, work or relationships calls for a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: Can't switch off after worrying? Worry Slot, Empty Slot is a new concept: 15 minutes to worry on paper on purpose, then 10 minutes of doing absolutely nothing. Practice in picking mental effort up, and then putting it down.

modalities.name: Benefit of the Doubt
modalities.tagline: When someone irritates you, make a generous guess and wish them well.
modalities.whatItIs: Benefit of the Doubt is a proposed practice halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and loving-kindness (metta) meditation, the practice of silently wishing people well. When someone's behavior irritates you, you first come up with one kinder explanation for it, a CBT habit, and then silently wish them well, as in metta, before deciding how to respond.
modalities.coreIdea: Irritation often rests on a quick, uncharitable guess about why someone acted as they did, and both CBT's search for other explanations and metta's goodwill work against it. Pairing the two in a set, two-step routine is meant to train a gentler first reaction without pretending the behavior was fine.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over six weeks you learn the routine in a weekly class with a meditation teacher or CBT-trained facilitator, and sit for ten minutes a day practicing it with people who irritated you that day. In the moment, step one is a generous guess, such as 'maybe they've just had bad news', step two is a silent phrase such as 'may your day get easier', and then you choose what to do, which can still mean saying no or setting a limit. Each evening you jot down one moment you used it and how the irritation shifted.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are quick to feel irritated or resentful with strangers, colleagues or family, and who want a structured way to soften their first reaction without becoming a pushover.
modalities.cautions: This is for everyday irritations, not for excusing mistreatment: if someone is harming you, a generous guess is no reason to stay in harm's way, and anger after abuse deserves care from a trained therapist. Wishing difficult people well can stir up anger or grief at first, so start with small annoyances; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Someone cuts in front of you. Before the anger lands, make one generous guess about why, then silently wish them a better day. Benefit of the Doubt is a new concept for people whose irritation flares fast and lingers.

modalities.name: Catch It Early
modalities.tagline: A short daily body-and-mind sweep for your personal early warning signs.
modalities.whatItIs: Catch It Early is a proposed practice halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and vipassana, or insight, meditation. It joins CBT's relapse-prevention plans, written lists of your own early warning signs and what to do about them, with the close, moment-by-moment noticing that insight meditation trains, in a short daily sitting.
modalities.coreIdea: Staying well after depression or anxiety often depends on spotting a dip early, and the first signs tend to be subtle: a tight jaw, a shrinking wish to see people, a flat 'what's the point'. Insight meditation trains exactly that kind of fine-grained noticing, so pairing a daily sweep with a written plan is meant to make early signs easier to catch while they are still small.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over about six sessions with a therapist, or a meditation teacher trained in CBT, who stays available afterward, you write your own list of early signs from past dips and a matching plan of small steps, such as calling a friend, protecting sleep or booking an appointment. Each morning you then sit for about 12 minutes, sweeping attention slowly through the body and then noting the mood and thoughts present without judging them, and you finish by checking your list. If two or more signs keep showing up for several days, you follow your plan.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have been through depression or anxiety and want to notice early if it is coming back, and meditators who want their practice to support a concrete self-care plan.
modalities.cautions: This supports ongoing care and never replaces it: keep your clinician's details on the plan, and get help promptly if signs escalate or thoughts of suicide appear. Meditation can occasionally bring up difficult experiences, so keep sittings short, and people with a history of psychosis or bipolar disorder should build the plan with their clinician; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Most dips in mood start small: a tight jaw, less wish to see anyone, a flat 'what's the point'. Catch It Early is a new concept: a 12-minute morning meditation sweep for your own early signs, linked to a written plan. For anyone who has had a dip before.

modalities.name: Prove-It Intervals
modalities.tagline: Hard intervals where 'I can't' thoughts get tested on the spot.
modalities.whatItIs: Prove-It Intervals is a new concept that brings the thought-testing of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) into interval training. The predictable discomfort of short, hard bouts brings up thoughts like 'I can't' or 'this is too much', and the easy recovery minutes become a lab for comparing those thoughts with what you actually did.
modalities.coreIdea: Interval training produces the same self-doubting thoughts on cue, at a controlled intensity, which may make them easier to catch and check in the moment. Each round turns a vague 'I can't' into a specific prediction, such as 'I'll have to stop by 40 seconds', that the next minute can confirm or contradict.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week, in a 30-minute session with a coach or class, you warm up and then do six rounds of one minute at a hard but sustainable effort, about 7 out of 10, on a bike or rowing machine, with two easy minutes between. Before each hard minute you write down your exact prediction, such as when you think you will have to stop, and in the easy minutes you compare it with what happened and note the thought that showed up. You finish with a cool-down and one written line on what the doubting voice got wrong, or right.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose self-doubt shows up as 'I can't' when things get hard, and who like short, structured workouts with a coach.
modalities.cautions: Hard bouts load the heart, so anyone with heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure should get medical advice first, build up gradually and keep easy days between sessions. The aim is to test self-doubt, never to override real warning signs such as pain, dizziness or chest discomfort, which mean stop; the concept is untested.
modalities.tweet: Mid-burst in a hard workout, your mind says 'I can't'. Prove-It Intervals, a new concept: before each burst, write down exactly when you think you'll have to stop, then check. For anyone who talks themselves out of hard things.

modalities.name: Prediction Scrimmage
modalities.tagline: A friendly team game for testing fears about other people.
modalities.whatItIs: Prediction Scrimmage is a proposed group practice halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and recreational team sport. Before a low-key, non-contact game played mostly at walking pace, each player writes down one fear about how others will react, such as 'if I drop the disc, they will be annoyed', and the game becomes a live test of it.
modalities.coreIdea: Team games constantly produce the very moments that social fears are about, such as making a mistake, asking for the ball or disagreeing, but in a playful, low-stakes setting. Turning those moments into planned experiments, and comparing predictions with what happened in a circle afterwards, offers quick evidence from real people.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week for eight weeks, ten to fourteen people meet for 75 minutes with a coach who has CBT-informed training, warm up together and play small-sided games of a self-refereed, non-contact disc or ball game at a brisk walking pace, with short jogs allowed but no sprinting. Before play, each person writes one prediction and one action to try, like asking for a pass or owning up to a drop, and after each game the group compares predictions with what actually happened. Results are tracked from week to week, so players can see how their predictions change.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who worry a lot about what others think, especially those who avoid groups but would rather learn by playing than by sitting in a room talking.
modalities.cautions: Quick turns, short jogs and catching bring a risk of sprains, falls and knocks, so warm up, keep the game non-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. Intense social fear or panic may need a therapist, and no one should be pushed into an experiment; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Pitch for a new game: Prediction Scrimmage. Before a walking-pace match, write down one fear about other people, like 'if I drop it, they'll be annoyed'. Play, then compare notes. Evidence from real teammates, for anyone who worries what others think.

modalities.name: One Block Further
modalities.tagline: Brisk walks that go a little further each week, into avoided places.
modalities.whatItIs: One Block Further is a proposed walking practice halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and endurance exercise. Each week's brisk walk goes a little further, or somewhere a little busier, than feels easy, so that stamina and the area you feel able to go grow together, one step at a time.
modalities.coreIdea: Endurance grows by adding a little distance at a time, and CBT's graded exposure shrinks avoidance the same way, by taking a slightly harder step once the last one feels manageable. Putting both on one walking plan is meant to give the body's progress and the mind's courage the same steady rhythm.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a CBT practitioner, or a workbook and a supportive friend, you list the places you have been avoiding, such as the busy high street, the bus stop two roads away or the park beyond the bridge, and plan a route that edges toward them over the weeks. Three times a week you walk briskly for 20 to 40 minutes at a pace where you can talk but not sing, adding a block, a busier stretch or a few minutes only when the last walk felt manageable, and staying in each new place until the first wave of nerves passes. A short note after each walk records the route and how it felt.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose world has shrunk because of anxiety, who stay close to home or avoid certain streets, and anyone rebuilding fitness and confidence together after a hard time.
modalities.cautions: If anxiety brings panic attacks or makes it hard to leave home at all, work with a qualified therapist rather than alone, and never push into a step that feels overwhelming. Check with a doctor before building up exercise if you have heart or other medical conditions, carry your phone and plan routes in daylight; the concept is untested.
modalities.tweet: Has anxiety shrunk the area you feel able to go? One Block Further is a new concept: brisk walks that go a little further, or a little busier, each week, building stamina and courage at the same steady pace. Small steps, one block at a time.

modalities.name: Corrections Welcome
modalities.tagline: Hear a coach's correction as useful information, not a verdict.
modalities.whatItIs: Corrections Welcome is a proposed practice that pairs a simple strength program with the thought work of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Lifting technique is learned through many small corrections, and each one becomes a chance to catch the harsh thought it sparks, such as 'I'm useless at this', and to practice answering it.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people hear any correction as a judgment on who they are, which can make them avoid feedback or give up. A coach's cue about a lift is about as neutral and small as feedback gets, so it is meant to offer a gentle, repeatable place to practice meeting correction with curiosity instead of shame.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week for eight weeks you train with a coach at moderate loads on a few basic lifts, and the coach gives one clear cue per set, such as 'knees out' or 'slower on the way down'. After each cue you note in a pocket notebook the first thought it brought up and, before the next set, write a more useful one, such as 'that's one thing to adjust'. Every few weeks you look over the notebook with the coach or a therapist and choose one correction outside the gym, at work or at home, to practice receiving the same way.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who freeze, argue or feel crushed when given feedback, including perfectionists who would rather not try than be corrected.
modalities.cautions: Learn technique gradually, keep loads moderate and breathe out on the effort rather than holding your breath, and get medical advice first if you have high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease. If feedback brings up intense shame or memories of harsh treatment, or low mood persists, talk to a therapist, since this untested idea is no substitute for care.
modalities.tweet: Do you hear every correction as a verdict on you? Corrections Welcome is a new concept: train with a coach who gives one clear cue per set, and practice answering the harsh thought each cue sparks. Low-stakes feedback, on repeat.

modalities.name: Pocket Calm
modalities.tagline: Link a dog's calming company to a cue you can carry.
modalities.whatItIs: Pocket Calm is a new concept for therapist-led sessions halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and animal-assisted therapy. It borrows cue-controlled relaxation from CBT, in which a settled state is repeatedly paired with a simple cue, and uses the calming company of a trained dog as that settled state, so you can later call up some of the calm without the dog.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people feel steadier with a friendly animal beside them, but that calm usually stays in the room. Pairing it again and again with a small cue of your own, such as a word and a press of thumb and finger, is meant to make it something portable you can use in stressful moments.
modalities.whatYouDo: In eight weekly 50-minute sessions, a licensed therapist and a certified dog-and-handler team meet you in a quiet room. While you sit with the dog and stroke it slowly, the therapist guides your breathing and attention until you feel settled, and each time you silently pair that state with your chosen cue, such as the word 'easy' and a gentle press of thumb and finger. In later sessions you practice calling up the cue with the dog across the room and then out of sight, and between sessions you try it in mildly stressful moments and note what helped.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel calmer around animals and want a way to take some of that calm into stressful moments, such as appointments, commutes or difficult calls.
modalities.cautions: Allergies, fear of dogs and bites are real risks, so contact is optional and supervised, hygiene rules apply, and the dog's comfort comes first: sessions stay short, it can rest or move away, and the handler ends any session if it shows signs of stress. The cue is a coping aid, not a replacement for care, so anxiety that persists or gets in the way of daily life calls for a licensed professional; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Calmer with a dog beside you? Pocket Calm is an untested idea: with a therapist and a trained dog, pair that settled feeling with a small cue, a word and a press of thumb and finger, then practice calling it up when the dog isn't there.

modalities.name: Four Corners Form
modalities.tagline: Four slow movements, each checking one part of the stress cycle.
modalities.whatItIs: Four Corners Form is a proposed movement routine halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and qigong. It pairs four slow, breath-paced movements with the four corners of the CBT cycle (body, feelings, thoughts and actions), so one short routine walks you through checking and adjusting each in turn.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT teaches that body sensations, feelings, thoughts and actions keep feeding each other, and qigong trains a calm, focused mind through slow, repeated movement. Giving each corner of that cycle its own movement aims to turn a mental checklist into a calm routine the body remembers.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn the routine in a six-week class with an instructor, who stays available for monthly check-ins, then practice it on your own for about 15 minutes a day, standing or seated. Each of the four movements carries one question: where is the tension, what is my mood from 0 to 10, what is my mind saying and is it fair, and what is one small helpful thing I could do next. You repeat the round three times, letting the breath slow, and end by writing down the action you chose.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like the logic of CBT but forget to use it when stressed, and people who want a gentle, structured routine that settles the body while organizing the mind.
modalities.cautions: The movements are gentle, but adapt them to your body and sit if standing is tiring, and anyone with a history of psychosis or another serious mental illness should get medical advice before starting qigong-style practice. It is an untested self-help idea, so keep up any care you already have and get professional help if distress persists.
modalities.tweet: Four slow movements, four questions: where is the tension, how is my mood, what is my mind saying, what is one helpful next step? Four Corners Form is a new qigong-style routine for people who forget their coping skills the moment stress hits.

modalities.name: All Ears Practice
modalities.tagline: Short, friendly chats where your attention stays on the other person.
modalities.whatItIs: All Ears Practice is a new concept for a small weekly group halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and intentional socializing. In short, friendly conversation rounds you practice keeping your attention on the other person's words and face rather than on how you are coming across, a shift that CBT for social anxiety puts at the center.
modalities.coreIdea: Social nerves tend to turn attention inward, onto a running commentary about how you look and sound, which leaves less of you for the conversation and can make it feel like a performance. Practicing attention outward in low-stakes rounds is meant to make conversation feel more like meeting someone and less like being watched.
modalities.whatYouDo: A group of eight to twelve meets for 90 minutes a week at a library or cafe, with a volunteer host trained in the format. In five-minute pairings you chat about an easy prompt, and whenever you notice your attention drifting to yourself, as in 'am I boring?', you bring it back to one detail of what your partner is saying; after each round, partners tell each other one thing they remember the other said. The evening ends with open mingling, where you try the same shift without the rounds.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel self-conscious in conversation and spend chats monitoring themselves, and anyone who leaves social events unable to remember much of what others said.
modalities.cautions: If social situations bring intense fear, panic or avoidance, or low mood persists, this may be social anxiety or depression, so talk to a doctor or therapist rather than rely on a group. Nobody has to share anything personal, and the idea itself is untested.
modalities.tweet: Spend conversations worrying how you're coming across? All Ears Practice is a new idea: short chats where you keep bringing attention back to what the other person says, then each name one thing you remember. Conversation as meeting, not performing.

modalities.name: Watch One Spot Change
modalities.tagline: Visit one natural spot weekly and note what has changed.
modalities.whatItIs: Watch One Spot Change is a proposed practice halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and time in nature. You choose one natural spot within easy reach, such as a tree, a hedge or a stretch of riverbank, return to it every week and record how it has changed, then set that record beside the 'nothing will ever change' and 'it's always like this' thoughts that low mood brings.
modalities.coreIdea: Low mood often speaks in absolutes ('always', 'never', 'nothing will change'), and CBT sees such thoughts as claims to be checked. A natural place that keeps changing week by week offers patient, visible evidence about change, gathered with your own eyes rather than argued for.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you walk at an easy pace to the same spot and spend about 20 minutes there, noticing and writing down or photographing what is different: buds, light, water level, birds, mud or fallen leaves. Before leaving you read one 'always' or 'never' thought from your week and write one sentence about what the spot suggests about it. A CBT practitioner or a workbook helps you set this up, and every month you look back over the notes and photos.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose low or anxious moods come with a strong sense that things will always be this way, and who like a slow, observant routine outdoors.
modalities.cautions: Choose an easy, safe spot, check the weather and tell someone where you are going, since slips, cold and getting lost are real risks even close to home. Weekly observation is no substitute for help when low mood persists or deepens, so talk to a doctor or therapist; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Low mood loves the words 'always' and 'never'. Watch One Spot Change is a new concept: visit the same tree or riverbank every week, note what is different, and set it beside those thoughts. Evidence about change, gathered with your own eyes.

modalities.name: Eyewitness Pause
modalities.tagline: Check an alarming thought against what your senses actually report.
modalities.whatItIs: Eyewitness Pause is a new concept halfway between the evidence-checking of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and sensory mindfulness. When an alarming thought tells you something about the present, such as 'everyone is staring' or 'something is wrong', you pause and gather plain sensory evidence like a careful eyewitness, then compare it with what the thought claimed.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT weighs thoughts against evidence, and sensory mindfulness offers the most direct evidence there is: what you can see, hear and feel right now. Separating the raw report of the senses from the story laid on top of it can show which parts of an alarming thought the moment actually supports.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn the steps from a short course or workbook and practice daily for 15 minutes, then use a three-minute version in the moment. When a thought alarms you, you write it in a note, then spend about a minute each listing only what you can see, hear and feel in your body, with no interpretation, as an eyewitness would. Then you read the thought again and mark which parts the senses support, which they do not, and what you would like to do next.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose anxious thoughts make confident claims about what is happening around them, and who want a quick, structured way back to the facts of the moment.
modalities.cautions: It is a gentle self-help idea, untested as a combination and not a stand-alone answer to panic disorder, PTSD or psychosis, which call for a qualified therapist. Some people notice heightened sensitivity to sights and sounds, or difficult memories, during sensory practice, so start gently and stop if it feels like too much.
modalities.tweet: When a thought says 'everyone is staring', be an eyewitness instead. Eyewitness Pause, an untested idea: for three minutes, note only what you see, hear and feel, then check which parts of the thought the moment supports. For minds that jump to conclusions.

modalities.name: The Reply Chorus
modalities.tagline: Sing a harsh thought once, then give the kind reply the chorus.
modalities.whatItIs: The Reply Chorus is a proposed songwriting practice halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and music. You take a harsh thought that keeps coming back and let it appear only once, as the song's opening line, while the chorus, the part you sing again and again, is a fairer, kinder reply built from the evidence.
modalities.coreIdea: Whatever goes in the chorus is what a song repeats and what tends to stick, so this method gives the hook to the answer rather than to the harsh thought. Hearing the old thought once and the reply on repeat is meant to make the balanced view the one that comes to mind first.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over six weekly sessions, one to one or in a small group led by a music therapist or songwriting coach with CBT training, you pick one thought, such as 'I always mess things up', set it to a simple tune as the opening line, and work with the leader on a short chorus that answers it, with no musical skill needed. Each week you add a verse with evidence or a memory that supports the reply, and you record the song on a phone. Between sessions you play it back and notice which lines of the chorus feel truest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find worksheets dry but love music, and people whose harsh inner voice already sounds like a song stuck on repeat.
modalities.cautions: Music can stir strong feelings, and for people prone to rumination a sad tune can deepen low mood, so keep the harsh thought to a single line, notice how the song leaves you and keep the volume moderate. Clinical work calls for a credentialed music therapist, and this untested idea is an add-on to professional care for serious depression, not a replacement.
modalities.tweet: In a song, the chorus is what sticks. The Reply Chorus is a new concept: sing a harsh thought like 'I always mess things up' just once, then write a chorus that answers it kindly and play that on repeat. No musical skill needed.

modalities.name: Two Loyalties Dialogue
modalities.tagline: Honor what your stuck pattern is loyal to, then choose your values.
modalities.whatItIs: Two Loyalties Dialogue is a new concept for therapy halfway between acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) and Coherence Therapy. It sees a stuck pattern as loyal to an old emotional purpose, such as staying small so as not to outshine a parent, and sets that loyalty side by side with what you value today, so you can make room for both and choose consciously.
modalities.coreIdea: Coherence Therapy holds that a symptom makes emotional sense, and ACT asks you to make room for inner experience while acting on your values. Naming the old loyalty with respect instead of fighting it, and setting it beside a value you live by now, may let the choice between them become truly your own.
modalities.whatYouDo: In fortnightly 60-minute sessions over about four months, a licensed therapist invites you to imagine in detail a day when the stuck pattern is simply gone, and to notice who or what you would seem to be leaving behind, which brings the loyalty into words, for example 'if I succeed, I leave my family behind'. You then say the old loyalty and the value it competes with out loud, and spend a few quiet minutes making room for the grief or guilt that comes with holding both. Between sessions you choose one small action that serves the value and notice, without judging, how the old loyalty reacts.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who know what matters to them yet keep acting against it, and who want to understand why before pushing harder.
modalities.cautions: Feeling an old loyalty fully can bring up grief or guilt about people you love, and making room for those feelings is not the same as putting up with harmful treatment from anyone. People with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should do this only with a licensed clinician experienced in trauma; the combination is untested and no replacement for well-tested care.
modalities.tweet: Know what matters to you, but keep doing the opposite? Two Loyalties Dialogue is a new therapy concept: find what the stuck habit is loyal to, like not outshining your family, honor it, and hold it beside what you value now. Then choose.

modalities.name: The Unfought Tremor
modalities.tagline: Let gentle tremors come and go, then stand and take one step.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unfought Tremor is a proposed body practice halfway between acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) and tension and trauma releasing exercises (TRE), in which the legs start to tremble on their own after tiring stretches. You practice the ACT skill of willingness, making room for what you cannot fully control, by letting gentle tremors come and go without fighting them, then stand up and take one small step toward something you value.
modalities.coreIdea: A tremor you can allow but not fully steer is a bodily stand-in for the feelings and thoughts we fight against, and noticing the mind's urge to stop or analyze it is practice in letting experience be. Standing up afterwards and naming one value-based action links that willingness directly to living by what matters.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the exercises with a certified provider, who stays available for check-ins, you practice at home for about 30 minutes: ten minutes of gentle leg-tiring stretches, then up to ten minutes lying on your back with bent knees, letting mild tremors run. When thoughts like 'this is weird' or 'make it stop' appear, you name them as thoughts and let the shaking continue only as long as it feels comfortable, stopping any time by straightening your legs. Then you stand, take a slow breath and say aloud one small action you will take today that matters to you.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry tension and find themselves fighting their own feelings, and who would rather practice acceptance through the body than through talking.
modalities.cautions: Tremor work can stir strong emotions or memories, so anyone with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis, bipolar disorder or another serious condition should learn it only with a clinically trained provider and alongside their own care. Ask a doctor first if you have epilepsy, are pregnant or are recovering from surgery or injury, and stop if you feel overwhelmed, in pain or panicky; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Acceptance, practiced through the body: The Unfought Tremor, a new idea. Tire your legs with gentle stretches, lie down and let the tremor come and go, then stand and name one thing you'll do today that matters. For people who fight their feelings.

modalities.name: The Sky Behind
modalities.tagline: Set each worry down, then sense the steady you behind them.
modalities.whatItIs: The Sky Behind is a new concept halfway between acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) and Focusing. It uses Focusing's first step, clearing a space by setting each current concern down at a little distance, to give a felt sense of what ACT calls the noticing self: the steady part of you that is there behind every passing thought and feeling, the way the sky is there behind the weather.
modalities.coreIdea: ACT holds that you are not your thoughts and feelings but the one who notices them, which is easy to say and hard to feel. Setting your concerns down one by one, and then sensing what is left when they are set aside, is meant to make that noticing self something you can feel in the body and come back to.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a listening partner or a Focusing-trained coach, you sit for about 30 minutes with your eyes closed. For each concern that comes up, such as a deadline, a quarrel or a worry about money, you acknowledge it, picture setting it down a little way off and say 'that's there', while your partner simply reflects back; when nothing more comes, you spend a few minutes sensing what it is like to be the one who set them all down, and find a word or image for it. You end by choosing one concern to pick back up, and one small step to take with it from that steadier place.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel there is no space between themselves and what they are going through, and who like quiet, body-aware ways of exploring.
modalities.cautions: Usually gentle, but turning attention inward can bring up strong feelings or painful memories, and some people find the felt sense hard to notice at first. People with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or a current crisis should work with a qualified therapist, as this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Ever feel there's no space between you and your worries? The Sky Behind is a new concept: set each concern down a little way off, one by one, then sense the steady you that is left, like sky behind weather. Then pick one back up from that steadier place.
